title: A Simple, Nearly-Optimal Algorithm for Differentially Private All-Pairs Shortest Distances

snippets.content: The all-pairs shortest distances (APSD) with differential privacy (DP) problem takes as input an undirected, weighted graph G = (V, E, w) and outputs a private estimate of the shortest distances in G between all pairs of vertices. In this paper, we present a simple Õ(n^{1/3} / ε)-accurate algorithm to solve APSD with ε-DP, which reduces to Õ(n^{1/4} / ε) in the (ε, δ)-DP setting, where n = |V|.

Our algorithm greatly improves upon the error of prior algorithms [CGK+23, FLL22], namely Õ(n^{2/3} / ε) and Õ(√n / ε) in the two respective settings, and is the first to be optimal up to a polylogarithmic factor, based on a lower bound of Ω̃(n^{1/4}) proven by [BDG+24]. In the case where a multiplicative approximation is allowed, we give two different constructions of algorithms with reduced additive error.

Differential privacy (DP) is a mathematical framework which quantifies the leakage of sensitive user information by an algorithm. Differential privacy has seen applications in industry and government agencies, with algorithms satisfying differential privacy being adopted by organizations such as Google [ABC+20, BDD+20, BBD+21], Microsoft [DKY17], and the US Census Bureau [GAP18, FMM19].

The all-pairs shortest distances (APSD) problem is a cornerstone of the field of graph algorithms and has been studied extensively. Given a connected graph G = (V, E, w) with n = |V|, the goal is to release the shortest distances in G between every vertex pair in V × V.

In 2016, Adam Sealfon [Sea16] was the first to study the application of differential privacy to the all-pairs shortest distances problem. We follow their DP framework where two graphs are neighboring if they share the same underlying unweighted graphs and their edge weight w differs by at most 1 in the l₁-distance.

In this paper, we improve upon the accuracy of the currently best-known algorithms for APSD with DP under both additive and mixed additive and multiplicative approximations. We show the additive approximation problem to be Θ̃(n^{1/4})-accurate by giving a nearly optimal algorithm which matches the known lower bound of Ω̃(n^{1/4}) up to a polylogarithmic factor.

We give a simple algorithm which releases a private approximation of the shortest path distances between all-pairs of vertices while only incurring an additive approximation. Given a pair of vertices, their private shortest distance is computed in one of two ways depending on the number of edges in a shortest path between them.

At a high level, our algorithms work by constructing a collection of spanning trees T, the shortest path distances in which can be used to estimate the shortest path distances in G for every pair of vertices with a multiplicative error.
In 2009, Hay et al. [HLMJ09] were the first to study differentially private graph algorithms by giving a mechanism to release a private estimate of the degree distribution in a graph.

Given a mechanism that takes as input a dataset and releases some aggregate statistical information about the dataset, the goal of differential privacy is to protect any one individual's privacy whose data is included in the dataset.

snippets.location: 3 A Nearly-Optimal Algorithm for General Graphs
snippets.content: In this section, we present a differentially private algorithm for APSD on general graphs which is Õ(n^{1/3}/ε)-accurate in the ε-DP case and Õ(n^{1/4}/ε)-accurate in the (ε, δ)-DP case.

Chen et al. [CGK+23] noted that the known lower bound of Ω̃(n^{1/4}) for the purely additive error does not apply in the setting where a multiplicative approximation is allowed. In this section, we adapt two existing mechanisms which output shortest distance estimates to the DP setting.
In this section, we give a simple construction of an algorithm with multiplicative error O(k log log n) which releases all-pairs distances with differential privacy.
In this section, we give an algorithm that modifies the oracle of Thorup and Zwick [TZ05] in order to apply Corollary 4.1 effectively.
The proofs presented are slightly modified from [Sea16] and are given for completeness.
Proof of Theorem 3.2: The algorithm is the same as Algorithm 1, except we run the ε/(4√(2s log(2/δ)))-DP algorithm from Lemma 3.2.
Proof of Theorem 4.2: The proof is identical to the proof of Theorem 4.1, except we run the ε/(2√2(k n^{1/k}) log(2/δ))-DP algorithm from Corollary 4.1.
Proposition E.1 and E.2 with their proofs.
**Definition 2.1.** Two graphs G = (V, E, w) and G' = (V, E, w̃) with equivalent topology are said to be neighboring if ||w − w̃||₁ ≤ 1.
**Definition 2.2.** The l₁ sensitivity of f : X → R^D is defined as Δ₁(f) := max_{X, X'} ||f(X) − f(X')||₁, where X, X' are neighboring datasets.
**Definition 2.3.** An algorithm M : X → R^D is said to be (ε, δ)-differentially private if, for all outcomes S ⊆ R^D and neighboring datasets X, X', P[M(X) ∈ S] ≤ e^{ε} · P[M(X') ∈ S] + δ.

**Lemma 2.1** (Basic Composition, [DMNS06, DL09]). Let ε, δ ∈ [0, 1] and k ∈ N. If we run k mechanisms where each mechanism is (ε/k, δ/k)-differentially private, then the entire algorithm is (ε, δ)-differentially private.

**Lemma 2.2** (Advanced Composition, [DMNS06, DR14]). Let ε, δ ∈ (0, 1] and k ∈ ℕ. If we run k mechanisms where each mechanism is (ε/(2√(2k log(2/δ))), δ/2k)-DP, then the entire algorithm is (ε, δ)-DP.

**Lemma 2.3** ([DMNS06]). Given any function f : X → ℝ^k, the Laplace mechanism on input X independently samples Y₁, ..., Y_k according to Lap(Δ₁(f)/ε) and outputs M_{f,ε}(X) = f(X) + (Y₁, ..., Y_k). The Laplace mechanism is ε-differentially private.

**Lemma 2.4** ([CSS11]). Let X₁, ..., X_t be independent random variables distributed according to Lap(b), and let X = X₁ + ... + X_t. Then for all γ ∈ (0, 1), with probability at least 1 − γ we have, |X| < O(b√t log(1/γ)).
**Lemma 2.5** ([CL06]). Let X ∼ Binomial(n, p) be a random variable, then, P[X ≤ E[X] − λ] ≤ e^{-λ²/2E[X]}.

**Lemma 3.1.** Let t ∈ ℕ, ε ∈ (0, 1], and γ ∈ (0, 0.5]. There is an ε-DP algorithm for computing d̃^{(t)}(u, v) for every u, v ∈ V such that with probability 1 − γ we have, max_{u,v ∈ V} |d̃^{(t)}(u, v) - d_G^{(t)}(u, v)| ≤ O(√t · log(n/γ)/ε).

**Lemma 3.2** (Theorem 4.1 in [Sea16]). Let T_z = (V, E, w) be a tree with root vertex z ∈ V, ε ∈ (0, 1], and γ ∈ (0, 0.5]. Then there is an ε-DP algorithm for releasing the distance between z and every u ∈ V that is O(log^{1.5}(n) · log(n/γ)/ε)-accurate with probability 1 − γ.

**Lemma 4.1** (Theorem 2 in [ACE+20]). For a parameter k ∈ ℤ⁺, there exists an algorithm that finds a collection T of k · n^{1/k} spanning trees of G such that for every u, v ∈ V, there exists a tree T ∈ T such that d_T(u, v) ≤ O(k log log n) · d_G(u, v).
**Lemma 4.2.** For all r ∈ [t], i ∈ [k-1], and w₁, w₂ ∈ A^r_i with w₁ ≠ w₂, C^r(w₁) ∩ C^r(w₂) = ∅.
**Lemma 4.3.** Each vertex u ∈ V has a uniform probability of being included in A^r_i and A_i for i ∈ [k-1] and r ∈ [t].
**Lemma 4.4.** |A_i| ≥ (t/4) · n^{1-(i+1)/k} for all i ∈ [k-1] with probability at least 1 − 1/(2n²).

**Theorem 3.1.** For γ ∈ (0, 0.5] and ε ∈ (0, 1], there is an ε-DP algorithm for computing all-pairs shortest distances that is O(n^{1/3} · log(n)^{11/6} · log(1/γ)/ε)-accurate with probability 1 − γ − 1/n².

**Theorem 3.2.** For γ ∈ (0, 0.5] and ε, δ ∈ (0, 1], there is an (ε, δ)-DP algorithm for computing all-pairs shortest distances that is O(n^{1/4} · log²(n) · √log(2/δ) · log(1/γ)/ε)-accurate with probability 1 − γ − 1/n².

**Theorem 4.1.** For γ ∈ (0, 0.5], k ∈ ℤ⁺, and ε ∈ (0, 1], there is an ε-DP algorithm to release all-pairs shortest distances that is (O(k log log n), O(k·n^{1/k}·log^{2.5}(n)·log(k)·log(1/γ)/ε))-accurate with probability 1 − γ.

**Theorem 4.2.** For any γ ∈ (0, 0.5], k ∈ ℤ⁺ and ε, δ ∈ (0, 1], there is an (ε, δ)-DP algorithm to release all-pairs shortest distances that is (O(k log log n), O(√k·n^{1/(2k)}·log^{2.5}(n)·log(k)·√log(2/δ)·log(1/γ)/ε))-accurate with probability 1 − γ.

**Theorem 4.4.** For γ ∈ (0, 0.5], ε, δ ∈ (0, 1], and k ∈ {2, ..., ⌊log(n)/log(2)⌋}, there is an (ε, δ)-DP algorithm that is (2k-1, O(√k·n^{1/(2k)}·log^{2.5}(n)·√log(2/δ)·log(k)·log(1/γ)/ε))-accurate with probability 1−γ−1/n².

**Corollary 4.1** (Theorem 4.2 in [Sea16]). Let T = (V, E, w) be a tree with ε ∈ (0, 1] and γ ∈ (0, 0.5]. Then there is an ε-DP algorithm for releasing all-pairs distances on T that is O(log^{1.5}(n)·log(n/γ)/ε)-accurate with probability 1 − γ.

Proof of Lemma 3.1: The algorithm constructs a noisy graph G̃ by adding Laplace noise to each edge weight from Lap(1/ε), then returns d̃^(t)(u,v) ← d_{G̃}^{(t)}(u,v). Each distance is the sum of at most t Laplace random variables. By Lemma 2.4 and union bound, the error bound holds.

Proof of Theorem 3.1: The algorithm samples a hitting set S of size s = n^{1/3}/log^{2/3}(n). For Case A (vertex in S intersects the shortest path), distances computed from shortest path trees have error O(s·log^{1.5}(n)·log(2sn/γ)/ε). For Case B (short path), error is O(√(n/s)·log^{1.5}(n)·log(1/γ)/ε). Balancing gives O(n^{1/3}·log^{11/6}(n)·log(1/γ)/ε).

Proof of Theorem 4.1: Let T be the tree-padding spanner from Lemma 4.1. For each tree, run the ε/(k n^{1/k})-DP algorithm from Corollary 4.1. By basic composition, releasing all distances is ε-DP. The error bound follows from Corollary 4.1's guarantee with a union bound over all trees.
Proof of Lemma 4.2: By contradiction: if C^r(w₁) ∩ C^r(w₂) ≠ ∅, there exists u with d(w₁,u) < d(u,a₁) ≤ d(u,w₂) < d(u,a₂) ≤ d(u,w₁), which is impossible.

Proof of Lemma 4.3: By induction on i. Base case i=k-1: single vertex picked at random, probability 1/n. Inductive step: P[u ∈ A^r_i] = P[u ∈ A^r_{i+1}] + P[u ∉ A^r_{i+1}]·P[u ∈ A^r_i - A^r_{i+1}] = n^{-(i+2)/k} + (1-n^{-(i+2)/k})·(n^{1-(i+1)/k}-n^{1-(i+2)/k})/(n-n^{1-(i+2)/k}) = n^{-(i+1)/k}.

Proof of Lemma 3.2: Split the tree into subtrees each with <n/2 vertices via centroids. Release distances between root and centroid and centroid and children with Laplace noise Lap(log(n)/ε). Recursively apply. Maximum recursion depth log(n), at most 2log(n) noisy distances per path. By Lemma 2.4 and union bound, error is O(log^{1.5}(n)·log(n/γ)/ε).

Proof of Corollary 4.1: Choose root z arbitrarily and use Lemma 3.2 to release distances from z to all vertices. For any x,y, d_T(x,y) = d_{T_z}(z,x) + d_{T_z}(z,y) − 2d_{T_z}(z,v_{x,y}) where v_{x,y} is the LCA. The total error is at most 4 times the bound from Lemma 3.2.

Proof of Theorem 3.2: Same as Algorithm 1 but using ε/(4√(2s log(2/δ)))-DP per tree via advanced composition (Lemma 2.2). Error from trees becomes O(√s·log^{1.5}(n)·√log(2/δ)·log(2sn/γ)/ε). Choosing s = √n/(log(n)·√log(2/δ)) gives final error O(n^{1/4}·log²(n)·√log(2/δ)·log(1/γ)/ε).

Proof of Theorem 4.2: Identical to Theorem 4.1 proof except using ε/(2√2(k n^{1/k})log(2/δ))-DP per tree via advanced composition (Lemma 2.2). Error becomes O(√k·n^{1/(2k)}·log^{2.5}(n)·log(k)·√log(2/δ)·log(1/γ)/ε).

Proof of Theorem 4.4: Same as Theorem 4.3 except using ε/(2√2(t·k)·log(2/δ))-DP per tree via advanced composition. Error O(√k·n^{1/(2k)}·log^{2.5}(n)·√log(2/δ)·log(k)·log(1/γ)/ε). Stretch analysis same as Theorem E.2 (2k-1).
Proof of Proposition E.1: (1-x)^{mx^{-1}log(n)} = n^{mx^{-1}log(1-x)}. Need mx^{-1}log(1-x) ≤ -m. Let f(x) = mx^{-1}log(1-x), lim_{x→0^+} f(x) = -m, f'(x)<0 for x∈(0,1).
Proof of Proposition E.2: (1) log(α^{1+λ}/γ) = (1+λ)·log(α/γ^{1/(1+λ)}) ≤ (1+λ)·log(α/γ) = O(log(α/γ)). (2) log(α/γ) = log(α) + log(1/γ) = O(max{log(α), log(1/γ)}) = O(log(α)log(1/γ)) as α, 1/γ ≥ 2.

Table 1: Summary of additive error terms for known algorithms compared to this paper's algorithms. We improve from Õ(n^{2/3}/ε) to Õ(n^{1/3}/ε) in ε-DP and from Õ(√n/ε) to Õ(n^{1/4}/ε) in (ε,δ)-DP.
Table 2: Summary of error bounds for algorithms with multiplicative approximation. We improve additive error from Õ(k·n^{1/2+1/(4k+2)}/ε) to Õ(k·n^{1/k}/ε) in ε-DP case.
